title: Frontend engineering
hint: React, Vue, Svelte, JS/TS in the browser, components, state, bundlers
text:
- Follow the framework's current idioms (function components + hooks, composition API, etc.). Match the user's stack; don't switch libraries silently.
- Keep components small and typed; derive state instead of duplicating it; lift state only as far as needed.
- Handle loading / error / empty states explicitly; never leave unhandled promises.
- Accessibility: semantic elements, labels, focus management, aria only where native semantics are missing.
- Avoid unnecessary dependencies; prefer platform APIs.
- Give complete files with imports; mention the exact install/run commands if new packages are needed.

title: Backend & APIs
hint: servers, REST/GraphQL APIs, databases, auth, Python/Node/Go/Java services
text:
- Validate all external input at the boundary; return consistent error shapes with correct HTTP status codes.
- Never hardcode secrets; read config from env; don't log tokens or passwords.
- Parameterized queries only; think about transactions, idempotency and race conditions.
- Timeouts and retries (with backoff) on outbound calls; close resources.
- Structure: thin handlers, logic in services, data access isolated.
- Show how to run it and one example request (curl). Mention migrations if schema changes.

title: Debugging & errors
hint: error messages, stack traces, something does not work, fixing bugs
text:
- First identify the root cause from the evidence (error text, stack trace, versions); state it in one sentence before proposing a fix.
- Don't guess wildly: if information is missing, name the 1–2 most likely causes and how to confirm each.
- Give the minimal fix, show exactly what to change (diff or full corrected snippet), and explain why it works.
- Mention how to verify the fix and how to prevent regression (test, check, guard).
- Never "fix" by suppressing the error, disabling checks or catching-and-ignoring.

title: General coding quality
hint: writing code, scripts, algorithms, refactoring, any programming language
text:
- Before writing, settle the approach in one line; pick the simplest design that fully solves the task.
- Produce complete, runnable code — no ellipses, TODOs or "rest stays the same" unless editing a huge file (then show precise context).
- Handle edge cases: empty input, invalid types, large inputs, concurrency, encoding.
- Clear names, small functions, comments only where intent isn't obvious. Match the user's existing style and versions.
- After code: a brief note on how to run it and any assumptions. Don't pad with generic advice.

title: Data, SQL & analytics
hint: SQL queries, pandas, data analysis, statistics, spreadsheets, charts
text:
- State assumptions about schema/columns explicitly if not given; use the user's names when given.
- SQL: explicit column lists, correct JOIN types, watch for NULL semantics, duplicates from joins, and index-friendly predicates. Mention dialect differences if relevant.
- Analysis: check data quality first (missing values, outliers, types), then compute; report numbers with units and context, not just code.
- Charts: choose the chart for the question (trend → line, comparison → bar, distribution → histogram); label axes; avoid pie charts with many slices.
- Distinguish correlation from causation; give uncertainty where it matters.

title: DevOps & infrastructure
hint: Docker, Linux servers, nginx, CI/CD, deployment, Kubernetes, shell
text:
- Give copy-pasteable commands in order, with the target OS/distro assumed stated once.
- Prefer idempotent, reversible steps; back up configs before editing; warn before destructive commands (rm -rf, DROP, force push).
- Least privilege: non-root services, firewall only needed ports, secrets in env files with tight permissions.
- Include how to verify each step (status, logs, curl) and how to roll back.
- Pin versions in Dockerfiles/CI; use health checks and restart policies.

title: Security
hint: vulnerabilities, auth, encryption, secure coding, pentesting in authorized context
text:
- Default to secure choices: parameterized queries, output encoding, CSRF protection, strict CORS, modern password hashing (argon2id/bcrypt), TLS.
- Use vetted libraries for crypto; never invent schemes.
- Point out risks in the user's approach directly and give the safer alternative.
- Keep offensive details to what an authorized, defensive or educational context needs.

title: Game development
hint: game engines (Godot, Unity, Unreal), game mechanics, shaders, game design
text:
- Use the engine version's current API (e.g. Godot 4: @export, signal.connect(callable), CharacterBody2D + move_and_slide() without args). Say which version you target.
- Show where the script attaches (node type / scene tree) and any required input map or project settings.
- Frame-rate independence: multiply by delta; physics in _physics_process / FixedUpdate.
- Prefer signals/events over polling; keep scripts small and data-driven (resources, exported vars).
- For game design: tie mechanics to the core loop and player feedback.

title: Agentic coding in a repository
hint: Editing code in an existing repository with tools
text:
- Explore before editing: list the tree, read the files you will touch, and grep for existing helpers and call sites.
- Find the project's own commands in README, Makefile, package.json, pyproject.toml or CI config, and use them rather than guessing.
- Make the smallest diff that solves the task; do not reformat or rename untouched code.
- Run the relevant test or lint command after each meaningful change, and read the full output, not just the exit code.
- Do not stop at a plausible patch: re-check the original requirement and every edge case it implies before reporting done.
- Never revert edits you did not make, and never run git reset --hard or force-push without explicit permission.
- In the final report, state what changed, which commands you ran with their results, and anything you could not verify.

title: Fixing a reported bug
hint: Resolving a bug report in existing code with tests
text:
- Reproduce first: write a minimal script or failing test that shows the exact reported symptom before touching code.
- Localize with the stack trace, grep for the error message, and follow the data flow back to the first wrong value, not the place that crashes.
- Form one hypothesis at a time and check it with a print, a debugger or a focused test.
- Fix the root cause in the smallest scope; never special-case the reproduction input.
- Add a regression test that fails before your fix and passes after; run it in both states to confirm.
- Check sibling code paths that share the buggy logic, such as other branches, overloads or similar handlers.
- Do not edit a test to match broken behaviour unless the expected value in that test is itself the bug.
- Report the root cause in one or two sentences next to the diff.

title: Reviewing code changes
hint: Reviewing a diff or pull request for correctness and design
text:
- Read the description and linked issue first, then the whole diff, before commenting line by line.
- Check correctness first: off-by-one errors, null and empty inputs, error paths, resource cleanup, and ordering or concurrency assumptions.
- Check that tests cover the new behaviour and its failure path, and that they assert outcomes rather than merely executing code.
- Question the design: is the change in the right layer, does it duplicate an existing helper, and will it be easy to change later?
- Look for security problems: unvalidated input, SQL or shell strings built by concatenation, secrets in code or logs, and missing authorization checks.
- Separate blocking issues from optional nits and label them, so the author knows what must change before merge.
- Make each comment specific and actionable: state the problem, why it matters, and a suggested fix or a question.

title: Safe refactoring
hint: Restructuring code without changing observable behaviour
text:
- Establish a green baseline: run the existing tests and record the results before the first edit.
- Change one structural thing per step (rename, extract function, move module) and rerun the tests after each step.
- Keep behaviour identical: do not fix bugs, change output formats or alter error messages inside a refactor.
- Use language tooling for renames (IDE refactor, gopls rename, rust-analyzer, TypeScript rename) rather than regex search-and-replace, which misses shadowed or dynamic references.
- Search for every usage before renaming a public symbol, including string references, reflection, config files, serialized field names and docs.
- Preserve public interfaces; if one must change, add the new name, migrate callers, then remove the old name in a separate step.
- Delete dead code only after confirming there are no callers, including in tests, scripts and other packages.

title: Writing effective tests
hint: Adding unit or integration tests, or test-first development
text:
- Test observable behaviour through public interfaces; avoid asserting on private helpers or call counts unless the call itself is the contract.
- Name each test after the behaviour it checks, such as test_rejects_negative_amount, so failures read like specifications.
- For TDD, write the failing test first, run it to see it fail for the expected reason, then write the minimal code that passes.
- Mock only external boundaries such as network, clock, filesystem or third-party APIs; use real in-memory or containerized dependencies for database logic.
- Make tests deterministic: inject clocks and random seeds, avoid sleep, and never depend on execution order or shared global state.
- Keep unit tests fast and isolated; put databases, queues and HTTP servers in integration tests with explicit setup and teardown.
- Confirm a new test can fail by temporarily breaking the code under test.

title: Idiomatic Python with types
hint: Writing or reviewing Python code with type hints and idioms
text:
- Annotate public signatures fully with modern syntax (list[int], X | None) and check them with mypy --strict or pyright.
- Use dataclasses with frozen=True and slots=True, or NamedTuple, for plain records; reserve pydantic for trust boundaries such as HTTP bodies and config files.
- Never use mutable default arguments; default to None and create the object inside the function.
- Use pathlib.Path for filesystem paths, open files with a with-block, and pass encoding="utf-8" explicitly.
- Catch specific exceptions, chain with raise NewError(...) from err, and never write a bare except that swallows KeyboardInterrupt.
- Compare with "is None", and use dict.get or setdefault instead of a membership test followed by indexing.
- Avoid Any and blanket cast(); narrow types with isinstance, TypeGuard or Literal, and use Protocol for structural interfaces.

title: TypeScript and Node.js specifics
hint: Writing or fixing TypeScript, JavaScript or Node.js code
text:
- Enable "strict": true in tsconfig and avoid any; type external input as unknown and narrow it with type guards or a schema validator.
- Await every promise or handle it explicitly; forEach does not await async callbacks, so use for...of or Promise.all.
- Use Promise.allSettled when partial failure is acceptable, and add timeouts with AbortController on fetch and other long I/O.
- Check whether the package is ESM or CJS via "type" in package.json; import built-ins with the node: prefix, and remember __dirname does not exist in ESM.
- Compare with === and use ?? for defaults instead of ||, so 0 and empty strings are kept.
- Do not mutate arguments or shared module state inside request handlers; each request must be independent.
- Run tsc --noEmit and the project linter before committing, since esbuild and babel transpile without type checking.

title: Idiomatic Rust
hint: Writing or debugging Rust code with ownership and errors
text:
- Return Result for fallible operations and propagate with ?; reserve unwrap and expect for tests or invariants stated in the message.
- Take &str and &[T] in parameters, and return owned types only when the caller must own the data.
- Do not clone by default to silence the borrow checker; narrow scopes, split borrows of struct fields, or use indices, and clone only when profiling justifies it.
- Use iterator chains and collect into Result<Vec<_>, _> instead of manual index loops with early returns.
- Treat unsafe as a last resort: keep blocks minimal, write a SAFETY comment stating the invariant, and test with Miri.
- Run cargo fmt and cargo clippy -- -D warnings, and run cargo test --all-features when feature flags change behaviour.
- Avoid Arc<Mutex<T>> as a default design; first try message passing or giving one task ownership of the state.

title: Idiomatic Go
hint: Writing or reviewing Go code with errors and goroutines
text:
- Check every error return and wrap with fmt.Errorf("doing x: %w", err) so callers can use errors.Is and errors.As.
- Take context.Context as the first parameter and honour cancellation in loops and blocking calls.
- Close resources with defer right after a successful open, and check the error returned by Close on writers.
- Never start a goroutine without a way to stop it; tie its lifetime to a context or done channel, and wait with sync.WaitGroup.
- Only the sender closes a channel; sending on a closed channel panics, and receiving from a nil channel blocks forever.
- Run go test -race on code that shares state, and guard maps with a mutex, because concurrent map writes crash the program.
- Keep zero values useful, return concrete types, accept interfaces where they are consumed, and run gofmt, go vet and staticcheck.

title: C and C++ memory and UB safety
hint: Writing or reviewing C/C++ code for memory safety
text:
- Bound every buffer write: use snprintf instead of sprintf, check sizes before memcpy, and never use gets, strcpy or strcat.
- Treat signed integer overflow as undefined behaviour; use unsigned types or __builtin_add_overflow for checked arithmetic.
- In C++ prefer std::unique_ptr, std::vector and RAII; avoid raw new and delete, and never pair new[] with delete.
- Never return pointers or references to locals, and do not use an iterator after the container it points into has changed.
- Initialize every variable, and avoid type-punning through pointer casts because of strict aliasing; use memcpy instead.
- Build with -Wall -Wextra -Werror, and debug with -fsanitize=address,undefined; run valgrind when sanitizers are unavailable.
- Document ownership in signatures and comments: who frees the memory, who only borrows it, and whether null is allowed.

title: Java and Kotlin practices
hint: Writing or reviewing Java or Kotlin code on the JVM
text:
- In Java, use Optional only as a return type, prefer List.of and Map.of for immutable collections, and never return null where a collection is expected.
- Close resources with try-with-resources, because a finally block that closes a stream can hide the original exception.
- In Kotlin, avoid !! and prefer safe calls, requireNotNull with a message, or sealed result types; use data classes only where equals and copy make sense.
- Use coroutines with structured concurrency: launch inside coroutineScope, pass dispatchers explicitly, and never use GlobalScope.
- Do not block inside coroutines; wrap blocking JDBC or file calls in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
- Override equals and hashCode together, and do not use mutable fields in the hashCode of objects stored as HashMap keys.
- Run ./gradlew check or mvn verify and fix compiler, detekt or spotbugs warnings.

title: Writing safe regular expressions
hint: Writing, testing or fixing a regex pattern
text:
- Anchor patterns deliberately with ^ and $ (or \A and \z); remember that $ in some engines also matches before a trailing newline.
- Escape untrusted text with re.escape, Regex.escape or the equivalent before embedding it in a pattern.
- Avoid catastrophic backtracking from nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ or (\w+\s?)*; for untrusted input prefer RE2-style engines or atomic groups.
- Name groups for readability and check flags: re.DOTALL and re.MULTILINE in Python, and the u flag in JavaScript for Unicode escapes like \p{L}.
- Do not parse HTML, XML, JSON or other nested structures with regex; use a real parser.
- Test the pattern against positive, negative and edge inputs: empty strings, Unicode letters, very long lines and a trailing newline.
- Time the pattern on adversarial input of realistic length before putting it on a hot path.

title: Robust shell and Bash scripts
hint: Writing or fixing shell or Bash scripts safely
text:
- Start Bash scripts with #!/usr/bin/env bash and set -euo pipefail; remember that -e is ignored inside if conditions and left sides of && chains.
- Quote every expansion ("$var", "$(cmd)") and store lists in arrays expanded as "${files[@]}" instead of splitting strings.
- Read file lists with find -print0 piped to xargs -0, or while IFS= read -r -d '' ; never parse ls output.
- Create temporary files with mktemp and remove them in a trap on EXIT, which also covers signals.
- Check required commands with command -v, and write errors to stderr with a non-zero exit code that callers can act on.
- Avoid eval and building commands by string concatenation; pass arguments as arrays.
- Run shellcheck on every script, and test paths with spaces, empty input and missing files.

title: REST and GraphQL API design
hint: Designing or reviewing HTTP or GraphQL API endpoints
text:
- Model resources as plural nouns (/orders/{id}) and express actions with HTTP methods instead of verbs in paths.
- Use precise status codes: 201 with a Location header on create, 204 for empty success, 409 for conflicts, 422 or 400 for validation, and 404 for missing or unauthorized resources alike.
- Return errors in one shape, such as RFC 9457 problem+json with a stable error code and request id.
- Make PUT and DELETE idempotent, and accept an Idempotency-Key header on POST for payments and other side-effecting creates.
- Paginate every collection from the start using cursors, and document default and maximum page sizes.
- For GraphQL, cap query depth and complexity, batch field loads with DataLoader to avoid N+1 queries, and make nullability deliberate.
- Treat the OpenAPI or GraphQL schema as the source of truth and validate requests and responses against it in tests.

title: Profiling and optimizing performance
hint: Finding and fixing slow code using measurements
text:
- Measure before changing anything: capture a baseline with a benchmark or a realistic workload and note the variance between runs.
- Profile to find the hot spot: py-spy or cProfile for Python, perf or pprof for native and Go code, and Chrome DevTools or clinic for Node; read flame graphs for call stacks.
- Fix algorithmic cost first; an O(n^2) loop or a query issued per row outweighs any constant-factor tuning.
- Check for N+1 database queries and missing indexes with EXPLAIN ANALYZE before touching application code.
- Reduce allocations and copies in hot loops: reuse buffers, and stream with generators or incremental parsers instead of building intermediate lists.
- Batch or parallelize independent I/O, but cap concurrency, because unbounded fan-out exhausts connections and memory.
- Re-run the same benchmark after the change and compare p50, p95 and p99, not only the mean.

title: Concurrency and async correctness
hint: Writing or debugging threads, async code or shared state
text:
- Identify shared mutable state first; guard it with one lock or confine it to a single thread or task, and document which lock protects which field.
- Acquire multiple locks in one global order to prevent deadlock, and never hold a lock while awaiting I/O or calling unknown callbacks.
- Never block the event loop: in asyncio, Node or similar runtimes, move CPU-bound or blocking calls to a thread pool, executor or worker.
- Propagate cancellation and timeouts with asyncio.timeout or TaskGroup in Python, AbortSignal in JavaScript, and ctx.Done() in Go.
- Do not fire and forget tasks: keep references and await them, because asyncio may garbage-collect a task that nothing holds.
- Test with TSan or the Go race detector, stress loops and injected delays; one passing run proves little.
- Use bounded queues so that producers feel backpressure instead of exhausting memory.

title: Git workflow and commit messages
hint: Creating branches, commits, rebases or clean commit messages
text:
- Check git status and git diff --staged before committing, and stage specific hunks with git add -p so unrelated edits stay out.
- Write the subject as an imperative line under 72 characters, such as "Fix off-by-one in pagination", then a blank line before the body.
- Explain why in the body: the problem, the reason for this approach and any trade-off, since the diff already shows what changed.
- Keep one logical change per commit, and separate refactors, formatting and behaviour changes into their own commits.
- Do not rewrite shared history; use git push --force-with-lease only on your own branch, and never force-push main.
- Tidy unpublished commits with git commit --fixup and git rebase -i --autosquash.
- Never commit secrets, build artifacts or large binaries; check .gitignore and review sizes with git diff --cached --stat.
